source_text: Si propter homines habitu abutuntur, impleant illum etiam in hoc, et ut apud ethnicos caput velant, certe in ecclesia virginitatem suam abscondant, quam extra ecclesiam celant. Timent extraneos, revereantur et fratres: aut constanter audeant et in vicis virgines videri, sicut audent in ecclesiis. Laudabo vigorem, si aliquid et apud ethnicos virginitatis nundinarint. Eadem nature foris quae et intus, eadem institutio apud homines et apud dominum eadem libertate constat. Quo ergo foris quidem bonum suum abstrudunt, in ecclesia vero provulgant? Exposco rationem. Utrumne ut fratribus suis placeant, an ut ipsi deo? Si ut ipsi deo, tam idoneus est ad conspicienda quaequae in occulto fiunt quam iustus ad remuneranda quae soli sibi fiunt. Denique praecipit, nihil debucinemus eorum quae apud illum mercedem merebuntur, nec ea ab hominibus compensemus. Quod si unius victoriati vel quameunque eleemosynae operationem sinistra conscia facere prohibemur, quantum tenebrarum circumfundere debemus cum tantam oblationem deo offerimus ipsius corporis et ipsius spiritus nostri, cum illi ipsam naturam consecramus? Ergo quod non potest videri propter deum fieri, quia sic fieri deus non vult, sequitur ut hominum gratia fiat, utique primo illicitum, ut gloriae libidinosum. Gloria enim illicitum est eis quorum probatio in omni humiliatione constat. Et si a deo confertur continentiae virtus, quid gloriaris quasi non acceperis? Si vero non accepisti, quid habes quod datum tibi non est? Hoc ipso autem constat a deo datam tibi non esse, quod illam non soli deo praestas. Videamus ergo quod humanum est, an firmum sit et verum.
thought_title: Veiling before God, not for human praise
orientation: Tertullian is addressing virgins who go unveiled in church, arguing that if they hide their virginity from outsiders they should hide it from fellow Christians too, since God alone should see what is done for him.
pass_a_gloss: If for the sake of men they misuse their dress, let them fulfill that also in this, and just as among the heathen they veil their head, certainly in the church let them hide their virginity, which they conceal outside the church. They fear strangers; let them also respect brothers: or let them consistently dare to be seen as virgins in the streets, just as they dare in the churches. I will praise their vigor, if they have also marketed something of their virginity among the heathen. The same nature outside which is also inside, the same institution among men and before the Lord stands by the same freedom. Why then do they hide their good outside, but in the church publish it? I demand a reason. Is it to please their brothers, or to please God himself? If to please God himself, he is as able to see whatever things are done in secret as he is just to reward the things that are done for him alone. Finally he commands that we should not trumpet any of the things that will merit a reward with him, nor should we have them repaid by men. But if we are forbidden to let the left hand know even a single penny's worth or any work of almsgiving, how much darkness ought we to pour around ourselves when we offer to God so great an offering of our very body and our very spirit, when we consecrate to him our very nature? Therefore what cannot be seen to be done for God's sake, because God does not wish it to be done that way, it follows that it is done for the favor of men, which is certainly first unlawful, as desirous of glory. For glory is unlawful for those whose testing consists in all humiliation. And if the virtue of continence is granted by God, why do you glory as if you had not received it? But if you have not received it, what do you have that was not given to you? But by this very fact it is established that it was not given to you by God, because you do not display it to God alone. Let us see therefore whether what is human is firm and true.

choices.why: Abutor takes the ablative of the thing misused; 'habitus' here means dress or outward appearance, which they use wrongly by going unveiled.
rejected: make bad use of their attire

choices.why: Nundinor means to trade or traffic; Tertullian is sarcastic about virgins selling or displaying their virginity for public notice.
Buccino means to sound a trumpet or proclaim loudly; it echoes Matthew 6:2 about not sounding a trumpet before you when giving alms.
Victoriatus was a small Roman silver coin; rendering it as 'penny's worth' conveys the smallness of the amount without anachronistic precision.
Libidinosus with the genitive means eager for or lusting after; here it characterizes the unlawful act as craving glory.

bible_refs.note: debucinemus echoes the trumpet imagery of almsgiving in Matthew 6:2.
sinistra conscia echoes 'let not your left hand know what your right hand does' in Matthew 6:3.
quid gloriaris quasi non acceperis and quid habes quod datum tibi non est echo Paul's questions in 1 Corinthians 4:7.

pass_b_english: If they misuse their dress for the sake of men, let them carry that through here as well: just as they veil their heads among the pagans, let them at least hide their virginity in the church, since they hide it outside the church. They fear strangers; let them also respect their brothers and sisters. Or let them be bold enough to appear as virgins in the streets, just as they dare to do in the churches. I will praise their vigor if they have marketed anything of their virginity even among the pagans. The same nature exists outside as inside; the same practice holds among men and before the Lord with the same freedom. Why, then, do they hide away their good outside but publish it in the church? I demand a reason. Is it to please their brothers, or to please God Himself? If it is to please God Himself, He is as able to see whatever is done in secret as He is just in rewarding what is done for Him alone. In fact, He commands that we should not trumpet any of the things that will earn a reward from Him, and that we should not have them repaid by men. If we are forbidden to let the left hand know about a single penny's worth of almsgiving, or any act of charity at all, how much darkness should we pour around ourselves when we offer God so great an offering as our very body and our very spirit, when we consecrate our very nature to Him? Therefore, what cannot be seen to be done for God's sake—because God does not want it done that way—follows as being done for human favor, which is certainly unlawful in the first place, as lustful for glory. For glory is unlawful for those whose testing consists in every kind of humiliation. And if the virtue of continence is given by God, why do you glory as if you had not received it? But if you have not received it, what do you have that was not given to you? By this very fact it is clear that it was not given to you by God, because you do not offer it to God alone. Let us see, then, whether what is human is firm and true.

problems.quote: which is certainly unlawful in the first place, as something desirous of glory
problems.source_quote: utique primo illicitum, ut gloriae libidinosum
problems.why: 'libidinosum' means 'lustful/inordinate desire' for glory, not merely 'desirous'; understates the force.
problems.fix: which is certainly unlawful in the first place, as lustful for glory
problems.ruling: Latin "libidinosum" means “lustful, inordinate desire”; translation “desirous” weakens the sense of illicit, covetous glory.

edits.old: which is certainly unlawful in the first place, as something desirous of glory
edits.new: which is certainly unlawful in the first place, as lustful for glory

fixed: Changed 'as something desirous of glory' to 'as lustful for glory' because 'libidinosum' means lustful or inordinately desirous, not merely desirous.

last_rejected.quote: let them also respect their brothers and sisters
last_rejected.why: Latin uses passive subjunctive ‘revereantur’ meaning ‘let them be revered’, not ‘let them respect’; agency is reversed.
last_rejected.fix: let them also be revered by their brothers (and sisters)
last_rejected.ruling: 'revereantur' is deponent: passive form, active meaning 'let them reverence/respect.' Agency correctly preserved by translator.
